title: From Idea to First Customer: The Only MVP Checklist a Startup Needs
excerpt: Most MVPs are neither minimum nor viable. The checklist we run inside Alttene — and with Alto Partners clients — to get from idea to a paying customer without burning six months on the wrong build.
content:
Every week someone shows us an "MVP" that took six months, has nine features, and no users. The letters have drifted from their meaning. A minimum viable product is not a small version of your grand vision — it's the cheapest honest test of the one assumption that kills you if you're wrong. Here's the checklist we actually run.

1. Write the kill assumption in one sentence

Every idea hides one assumption that, if false, makes everything else irrelevant. For Koffeechat it was: will two strangers actually show up to a scheduled short conversation? Not the matching algorithm, not the app — showing up. Name yours before you build anything, because the MVP exists only to test that sentence.

2. Test it without software if you possibly can

Our first version of almost everything is a spreadsheet, a form, and some manual labor behind the curtain. Concierge the service by hand for ten users. Sell the product with a landing page before it exists. Software makes things scale; it doesn't make things true. Find truth first — it's cheaper by a factor of a hundred.

3. Charge money embarrassingly early

Free users are applause; customers are evidence. The moment anything works, ask someone to pay — even a token amount. The conversation changes instantly: politeness falls away and you hear what the product is actually worth. Ten paying customers teach you more than a thousand signups ever will.

4. Pick one number and one narrow door

One metric that proves the assumption (completed chats, repeat orders, paid conversions — not downloads). One narrow audience most likely to feel the pain (not "professionals" — "first-year analysts in Lagos trying to break into IB"). Narrow doors open; wide doors are walls. You can widen later from a beachhead you actually hold.

5. Set the verdict date before you start

Decide up front: "By March 31, either 30% of matched pairs complete a chat, or we change course." Without a date, hope does the deciding, and hope always votes to keep going. A kill criterion isn't pessimism — it's what lets you bet aggressively, because the downside is capped at one honest experiment.

The whole checklist in one line

One assumption, tested by hand, priced in real money, measured by one number, judged on a date. Everything else — the logo, the stack, the pitch deck — can wait for customer number two.
author: Alttene Team
